title: Anchorage: Knik Glacier Helicopter Tour with Landing
cancellationDescription: Cancel up to 24 hours in advance for a full refund
description:
Fly from Alaska Glacier Lodge, a scenic 1-hour drive north of Anchorage (transfers available for purchase), to the spectacular Knik Glacier.
Soar over the beautiful valley and search the landscape for local wildlife, including moose, mountain goats, bands of Dall sheep, and bears.

Your experienced Alaska pilot/guide will land your helicopter in the middle of Knik Glacier, where you'll have the opportunity to explore the thousand-year-old ice during the 30-minute stop.
Enjoy the bright-blue melt pools, massive crevasses, and the unique ice formations created by the water, wind, and sun. Mark the moment with a photo, or simply savor the peace of being in a secluded Alaskan glacier.

Conclude with a 15-minute flight back to your starting point, flying over a glacier river flowing rapidly through the Knik Valley.
highlights: Thirty minutes of flightseeing over the Knik River valley and the Chugach Range
Thirty minutes on the surface of Knik Glacier, ice roughly a thousand years old
Crevasse fields, meltwater rivers and glacier waterfalls seen from a few hundred feet
Pilot-narrated wildlife spotting — moose, black bear, Dall sheep and mountain goats
The cheapest landing tour from the Knik River base, and the highest-rated on the site
excludes: Hotel pickup and drop-off from Anchorage

Flights are weather-dependent. Low cloud, wind or icing will delay or cancel a departure, and morning slots historically fly more reliably than afternoon ones.

fullDescription: This is the shortest, cheapest and best-reviewed way to stand on Knik Glacier. You check in at Alaska Glacier Lodge on East Knik River Road — about an hour's drive north of Anchorage — and fly out in a light helicopter with a pilot who narrates the whole way.

The flight runs roughly thirty minutes each way over the Knik River valley and into the Chugach, low enough to pick out crevasse fields, meltwater rivers and waterfalls running off the ice. Pilots watch for moose, black bears, Dall sheep and mountain goats on the valley walls, and will circle for a better look when something is worth seeing.

Then the skids touch down on the glacier itself and you get thirty minutes on ice that fell as snow around a thousand years ago. It is quiet in a way that is difficult to describe until the rotor winds off. Bring sunglasses — the glare off clean ice on a bright day is severe.

The lodge does not include transport from Anchorage in the price, but transfers can be bought separately: call the operator on 907-272-7777 after you have booked to arrange one. Most guests drive themselves, and the Old Glenn Highway approach is worth the trip on its own.

faq.q: Does this tour leave from Anchorage?
faq.a: No. Every helicopter on this tour lifts off from Alaska Glacier Lodge on East Knik River Road, about an hour's drive north of Anchorage. The tour is sold as an Anchorage experience because that is where guests are staying, but the drive out is yours to make unless you buy a transfer separately — call 907-272-7777 after booking.

faq.q: How long do you actually spend on the glacier?
faq.a: Thirty minutes on the ice, plus roughly thirty minutes of flying split between the trip out and back. The whole booking runs about an hour from lift-off to landing, on top of the drive and a check-in you should arrive early for.

faq.q: What happens if the weather is bad?
faq.a: The flight does not go. Helicopters need cloud ceiling and visibility, and Alaskan cloud builds through the day, so this is a real risk rather than a formality. Book a morning slot and, if you can, book it early in your trip so there is room to be rescheduled.

faq.q: Is it cold on the glacier in summer?
faq.a: Colder than the valley you drove up. The ice generates its own chill and there is usually a breeze moving across it. A fleece or light insulated jacket is enough on a bright July day; in shoulder season bring gloves and a hat.

faq.q: Can children do this tour?
faq.a: Yes, and families make up a fair share of the bookings. What matters is that everyone can climb into and out of the aircraft unaided and walk a short distance on uneven ice in proper shoes.

title: Anchorage Area: Helicopter and Glacier Dogsled Tour
cancellationDescription: Cancel up to 24 hours in advance for a full refund
description:
Soar over Alaska on a spectacular helicopter ride above glaciers and icebergs. Search the skyline for moose, black bears, Dall sheep, and mountain goats. Land on a glacier snowfield and enjoy a whole hour with Alaskan sled dogs and their mushers who live here all summer long.
Take the dog team for an exhilarating dog sled ride through snow, surrounded by amazing scenery. Overboots so your shoes stay dry, extra jackets and warm gear can be provided. Stand on the runners and mush your own dog team, or sit on the sled and let the mushers run the team.
The length of this tour makes it perfect for any traveler. After the dogsled tour, meet the canine athletes that pulled your sled, listen to stories about running sled dog races over 1,000 miles long, meet the puppies and take pictures with your favorite dogs.
After the dog sled experience, take a helicopter ride over the lower glaciers where you can see the blue melt pools and the crevasses on your way back to the lodge.

Weather can affect the operation of this tour due to the high-altitude location. If your tour is affected, you will always be given the option to rebook a different tour (which may involve a partial refund or increased charge depending on the newly chosen experience), reschedule for a different time or day, or cancel for a refund.

fullDescription: Dogsledding on real snow in the middle of an Alaskan summer only works if you get above the snowline, which is why this tour begins in a helicopter. Thirty minutes of flying takes you from the Knik River valley over the Chugach Range, past Knik Glacier and Lake George, to a snowfield camp that stays frozen all season.

On the ice you get a full hour with the dogs — long by the standards of glacier dogsled tours, most of which give you fifteen or twenty minutes. That is enough time to take the team out for a genuine run rather than a lap, meet the mushers who live at the camp through the summer, and spend time with the dogs off the line.

The operator makes a point of its weather record: flying out of the Knik River valley, it claims a better dispatch rate than glacier dogsled operations working out of Girdwood, Seward, Juneau, Haines or Skagway. It is an operator claim rather than a published statistic, but the inland valley genuinely sees less coastal cloud than Turnagain Arm does.
Overboots for the snow are handed out before you fly. Everything else — warm layers, hat, sunglasses — is on you.

faq.q: Are the dogs kept on the glacier all summer?
faq.a: Yes. The camp is staffed through the season by mushers who live alongside the team, and the dogs are worked and rested on a schedule that suits the snow rather than the tour timetable. You will meet the handlers as well as the dogs.

faq.q: How does an hour compare to other glacier dogsled tours?
faq.a: It is roughly three to four times longer. Most helicopter dogsled products in Alaska allocate fifteen to twenty minutes of sled time; this one gives sixty. It is also why the price sits well above a straight landing tour.

faq.q: Is this better than the Girdwood dogsled tour?
faq.a: They are different products. This one gives more time with the dogs and departs from the inland Knik valley; the Girdwood tour flies to Punchbowl Glacier at 3,200 feet with Mitch Seavey's IdidaRide team and takes 85 minutes on the snow. Direction of travel from Anchorage is usually the deciding factor — north or south.

faq.q: Can I take a backpack?
faq.a: No. Backpacks, weapons, sharp objects and drones are all refused. Take a phone or camera in a pocket and leave the rest in the car.

faq.q: Will my whole group fly together?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Helicopters are loaded to a weight-and-balance plan, so a larger party may be split across two departures and reunited at the camp.

fullDescription: This is the cheapest glacier landing on the site and, measured in minutes on the ice, one of the most generous: forty to forty-five minutes of flying and forty-five minutes on Knik Glacier itself. Outbound Heli Adventures flies from its own pad at the end of Lindsey Circle in Palmer, so you are dealing with the operator directly rather than checking in at a lodge.

Knik is one of the largest glaciers in southcentral Alaska — around twenty-five miles long and more than five miles across at its widest — and the flight out gives you enough time over it to understand the scale before you land on it. Pilots point out salmon in the river below, moose in the flats and Dall sheep on the valley walls.

Microspikes are handed out for the ice, which matters: forty-five minutes is long enough to walk somewhere rather than stand near the aircraft, and clean glacier ice is slick. Groups are capped at seven.
Weight rules here are stricter and more explicitly published than on most listings, and they are worth reading before you book — see the practical notes below.

faq.q: Why is this the cheapest tour on the site?
faq.a: Shorter flight time and a simpler product. There is no dogsled camp, no guided hike and no lunch — it is the aircraft, the pilot, the glacier and forty-five minutes to walk around. It also happens to give more ice time than tours costing 50 percent more.

faq.q: What are the weight limits?
faq.a: A hard 300 lb limit per seat, plus a combined limit of 650 lbs in the three-passenger helicopter and 900 lbs in the four-passenger one. If your party exceeds an aircraft's total and needs a second helicopter, there is an additional $350 charge. Weigh in honestly at booking — it is a flight-safety number, not a formality.

faq.q: Where exactly is the departure point?
faq.a: The operator's own pad at the very end of Lindsey Circle in Palmer, about an hour's drive north of Anchorage. Helicopters depart from that location, so there is no shuttle leg between check-in and the pad.

faq.q: Do I need my own crampons?
faq.a: No. Microspikes are included and handed out before you walk on the ice. Bring shoes sturdy enough to take them — trainers with a soft sole are not ideal.

faq.q: How big is Knik Glacier?
faq.a: Around twenty-five miles long and over five miles across at its widest, which makes it one of the largest glaciers in southcentral Alaska. It feeds the Knik River, which runs another twenty-five miles down to Knik Arm.

fullDescription: The Grand is the same operator's one-hour Knik landing tour extended into a two-hour flight with three separate touchdowns. That structure is the point: instead of one glacier surface, you see the ice from three different vantages, including a remote peak that looks down the length of Knik Glacier.

One landing puts you on the glacier proper, among the azure melt pools that open across the surface through summer as the ice drains. Another puts you somewhere you could not otherwise reach on foot — a ridge or a high shoulder — with a guided walk rather than a stand-and-photograph stop.

Because it is helicopter-access throughout, you get the terrain without the approach: no eight-hour hike in, no river crossing, no scramble. It is the tour to pick if the reason you want a glacier is the view of it rather than the walk on it.

Check in at Alaska Glacier Lodge on East Knik River Road thirty minutes before your scheduled departure. As with every flight from this base, the drive out from Anchorage is about an hour and is not included.

faq.q: What makes this different from the standard Knik landing tour?
faq.a: Time and touchdowns. The standard tour is one hour with a single glacier landing; the Grand is two hours with three, including a peak landing and a guided walk. You pay roughly 45 percent more for double the airtime.

faq.q: Are the three landing spots always the same?
faq.a: No. Pilots choose sites on the day for weather, snow and surface conditions. The shape of the tour — glacier surface, high vantage point, and a third stop — holds, but the exact places change.

faq.q: Is the guided hike difficult?
faq.a: It is a walk rather than a hike in the mountaineering sense: short distances on uneven ice and rock, at a pace set by the group. Proper closed shoes matter more than fitness.

faq.q: What are the melt pools?
faq.a: Through summer, meltwater collects in depressions on the glacier surface and drains through it, leaving pools of a startling turquoise. They are at their most vivid from late June through August, and they refreeze and vanish in winter.

faq.q: When should I arrive?
faq.a: Thirty minutes before your scheduled departure, at the lodge front desk. Budget an hour on top of that for the drive from Anchorage, plus margin — the Old Glenn Highway is not a road to rush.

fullDescription: Paddleboarding on a glacier sounds like a stunt until you see the pools. Through summer, meltwater collects on and beside Knik Glacier in basins deep enough and calm enough to paddle, hemmed in by walls of blue ice. This tour flies you to one of them and puts you on the water in a dry suit.

It is a four-hour outing built around that, with guides who carry bear-safety and medical rescue gear and who run the safety brief properly. Dry suit, flotation device, leash, throw rope, board, paddle and microspikes are all provided; lunch is included. Some guests get in the water as well as on it, which is a genuine cold-shock experience and entirely optional.

This is the most physically demanding tour on the site after the ice climbing. The operator asks for a moderate level of fitness and a tolerance for extreme cold, and it means both: you are outdoors for up to four hours on and around ice, in weather that can turn.

At $1,416 per person it is also the joint most expensive. What you are buying is a half-day with guides on a glacier that almost nobody else is standing on, not a flightseeing trip with an activity attached.

faq.q: Do I need to have paddleboarded before?
faq.a: No. The water is flat and enclosed and the guides run a full brief, so complete beginners manage. Balance and cold tolerance matter more than technique — you are on a board in a dry suit beside a wall of ice.

faq.q: Is the dry suit enough to keep me warm?
faq.a: A dry suit keeps water out; it does not insulate on its own. Wear warm base layers underneath — a thermal top and bottom plus wool socks — and you will be comfortable. In just a t-shirt you will not be.

faq.q: Do I have to get in the water?
faq.a: No. The plunge is optional and plenty of guests skip it. If you do go in, expect genuine cold shock: this is meltwater a few degrees above freezing, not a swim.

faq.q: Why does it cost so much more than a landing tour?
faq.a: You are buying four hours of guided time, a full kit of technical gear, lunch and a considerably longer helicopter commitment. A straight landing tour is one hour of aircraft and thirty minutes on the ice.

faq.q: What if the pool isn't there?
faq.a: Meltwater pools form and drain with the season and the weather, so guides pick a site on the day. Early season and after a cold snap the options are fewer; midsummer is when the pools are at their best.

fullDescription: This is the southern alternative to the Knik River dogsled tours, and the only one on the site that flies out of Girdwood — forty miles down the Seward Highway from Anchorage, about forty-five minutes' drive. You check in at the Alpine Air hangar at Girdwood Airport and fly up into the Chugach.

The destination is Punchbowl Glacier, a snowfield sitting at around 3,200 feet, where Mitch Seavey's IdidaRide kennel keeps a summer camp. Seavey is a three-time Iditarod champion, and the dogs on the glacier are working animals in their off-season conditioning rather than a display team.

The glacier experience runs about ninety minutes, of which roughly eighty-five are on the snow: a sled run with a musher guide, a tour of the camp, and time with the dogs. Sled dog puppies live at the camp through the season, and meeting them is a scheduled part of the visit rather than a happy accident.

Outer layers and boots are provided at the hangar, so you do not need to arrive dressed for a glacier. Groups are capped at ten. If you are a party of two or three, be aware that a sled run needs four people to launch — the operator may move you to another departure with other travellers.

faq.q: Where is Punchbowl Glacier?
faq.a: In the Chugach Mountains above Girdwood, at around 3,200 feet. It holds snow through the summer, which is what makes a June or July dogsled run possible. You cannot drive or walk to the camp — the helicopter is the access.

faq.q: Are these real racing dogs?
faq.a: Yes. The camp is run by Mitch Seavey's IdidaRide kennel; Seavey has won the Iditarod three times, and the glacier camp is part of the team's summer conditioning. The mushers on the ice work with these dogs year-round.

faq.q: How far is Girdwood from Anchorage?
faq.a: About 40 miles and roughly 45 minutes down the Seward Highway, which runs along Turnagain Arm and is one of the best drives in the state. Transport is not included but the operator can arrange a shuttle for an extra fee — call them after booking.

faq.q: What if there are only two of us?
faq.a: A sled run needs four people to launch. The operator may contact you and move you to another convenient departure with another group. Solo travellers should call ahead and be added to an existing reservation rather than booking blind.

faq.q: Do I need my own winter clothing?
faq.a: No. Outer layers and boots are provided at the hangar. Bring warm layers to wear underneath, plus gloves and sunglasses — the glare off a snowfield at 3,200 feet is strong even under cloud.

description:

fullDescription: Ninety minutes of flying and two landings — one on glacier ice and one on a high alpine ridge or a remote mountain lake. It is the longest pure flightseeing tour on the site and the only one that puts you down on two entirely different kinds of terrain in a single trip.

The route runs out of Girdwood Valley and into the Chugach, over icefields, crevasse fields and, from spring through late summer, meltwater pools scattered blue across the white. Pilots narrate the whole way and watch for moose, bears and mountain goats on the slopes below.

The second landing is what distinguishes it. A glacier landing gives you ice; a ridge or lake landing gives you the view back across the icefield you have just flown over, which is a different and in some ways better photograph. Which one you get depends on conditions on the day.

This is a good fit for photographers and for anyone who would rather spend the money on airtime than on an activity. Arrive fifteen minutes early for the safety briefing. Note the two-passenger minimum: solo travellers need to call rather than book online.

faq.q: What are the two landings?
faq.a: One on glacier ice, where you spend around thirty minutes, and one on either a high alpine ridge or a remote mountain lake. The second site is picked on the day for weather and surface conditions.

faq.q: Can I book as a solo traveller?
faq.a: Not directly online unless the departure already has another booking. There is a two-passenger minimum, so call the operator — they will tell you which slots already have someone on them.

faq.q: Is 90 minutes worth the extra money over a one-hour tour?
faq.a: If flying is the point, yes. You get half again the airtime, a second landing on completely different terrain, and a route through the Chugach rather than a single valley. If standing on ice is the point, a Knik landing tour gives you more glacier time for less money.

faq.q: When are the meltwater pools visible?
faq.a: Spring through late summer. They form as the surface drains and refreeze in winter, so a September flight will show fewer than a July one.

faq.q: How early should I arrive?
faq.a: Fifteen minutes before the flight time for the briefing, plus the drive: Girdwood is 40 miles south of Anchorage on the Seward Highway, about 45 minutes without stops.

title: Anchorage: Knik Glacier Helicopter and Hiking Adventure Tour

description:
Feed your adventurous heart on this round-trip helicopter ride and hiking tour from Anchorage. Explore the lush Alaskan wilds from the sky and on land, including the Chugach Range, Knik Glacier, Lake George, and more. Enjoy a flexible trip that can be customized to your interests.

Start your trip by considering the best location for your hike and the itinerary with your guide. There are dozens of incredible high-alpine locations that are ideally suited for heli-hiking. Your guide will be there to help satisfy your interests.

After deciding on your ideal hiking experience, you’ll board the helicopter and be whisked to the location. Upon arrival, your guide will help you out of the helicopter, which will then zip back to the lodge.

Complete silence will quickly surround you. From here, take in the one-of-a-kind scenery and go explore with your guide. You’ll be traveling in a group size that ensures an optimum wilderness experience with a minimized human impact.

This tour is all about you, so ask when you would like to stop, take a break, snap some pictures, or run up the ridge to see what is back there ─ more mountains and glaciers, but go for it.

Your guide will be perfectly happy taking it easy and waiting with you for the perfect light, that cloud to move into position, or for wildlife to get just a bit closer, all while looking out for your safety.

At the end of your adventure on land, you’ll return round-trip to the take-off location.

faq.q: How hard is the hike?

faq.q: How is this different from the Grand tour's guided walk?

faq.q: Do I need hiking experience?

faq.q: Is lunch included?

fullDescription: Ice climbing on Knik Glacier, reached by helicopter, with no previous experience required. You meet your guide at Knik River Lodge, fly over the glacier, and land beside features that would take most of a day to walk to — frozen waterfalls, crevasse walls and seracs, all a short distance from where the helicopter puts you down.

You get up to four hours on the ice with an instructor — two of them in winter — and all the climbing equipment is provided: boots, crampons, axes, harness, helmet and ropes. The difficulty is yours to set. Guides will find something gentle and confidence-building or something steep, and most groups do both across an afternoon.

In winter the tour adds glacier ice cave exploration, which is only possible once meltwater channels have frozen solid and the surface is stable. That makes this one of the few tours on the site with a genuinely better winter version rather than a reduced one.

Lunch is included and eaten on the glacier — beside it in winter. Bring warm and waterproof clothing: the operator provides the technical gear but not the layers, and standing around on ice between climbs is where people get cold.

faq.q: Do I need to have climbed before?
faq.a: No. The instructor teaches the technique on the ice and sets the difficulty to your level. What you need is a moderate level of fitness and a willingness to be cold and wet for a few hours.

faq.q: What is included in the equipment?
faq.a: Everything technical: ice axes, crampons, harness, helmet and ropes. Not included is clothing — warm and waterproof layers are explicitly your responsibility, and the listing says so.

faq.q: Is the winter version better?
faq.a: Different, and arguably yes. Winter adds glacier ice cave exploration, which is only possible once the meltwater channels freeze solid, and puts a second instructor on the ice. Lunch moves to beside the glacier rather than on it.

faq.q: How much of the four hours is climbing?
faq.a: Up to four hours on the ice in total, which includes the walk-in from the landing site, the teaching, the climbing itself and lunch. The actual time on the ropes depends on the group.

faq.q: Why does this tour have no reviews yet?
faq.a: It is a low-volume specialist product from an operator whose other tours on this site carry 85, 63 and 24 reviews at 4.93 to 4.99. You are booking on the operator's record rather than this listing's, which is worth weighing.
